concepts.title: Mesopotamia and Its Urbanisation
concepts.definition: Mesopotamia, the land between the Euphrates and Tigris rivers, saw the earliest urbanisation from about 3000 BCE, where temples and ziggurats, specialised craftsmen, trade and writing organised city life in Sumer, Akkad, Babylon and Assyria.
concepts.key_idea: Urban populations could only be sustained by intensive agriculture with irrigation, and the surplus fed kings, priests, officials and craftsmen who did not grow food.

concepts.title: Cuneiform Writing and Its Uses
concepts.definition: Writing began in Mesopotamia as cuneiform wedge shaped signs pressed on clay tablets, first used for record keeping of goods and debts, and later for letters, laws, literature like the Epic of Gilgamesh and school texts, with literacy remaining the monopoly of scribes.
concepts.key_idea: Tablets of clay were cheap and durable, which is why thousands of cuneiform tablets survive to tell us of daily life, contracts and royal deeds.

concepts.title: Life in the City: Kings, Law and Society
concepts.definition: Mesopotamian cities were ruled by kings who built temples and fought wars, law codes like that of Hammurabi regulated society with punishments by status, and family life, property, slavery and trade are known from legal texts and archaeology.
concepts.key_idea: The law code of Hammurabi shows a society divided by rank, where the same offence drew different punishments for nobles, commoners and slaves.
